title: Zagreb Orders the Guns Silent: The Washington Turn for Herceg-Bosna
sources: Washington Agreement on the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (1 March 1994)
ICTY Prlić et al. Trial Judgment (IT-04-74-T), end-of-conflict findings
content:
In the late winter of 1994, the Croat-Bosniak war that had ravaged central Bosnia and Herzegovina for a year was brought to an abrupt close — not primarily by the exhaustion of the combatants, but by a decision taken in Zagreb. Under intense American pressure, and with Croatia’s own strategic interests pointing toward partnership with the Bosnian government against the Serbs, President Franjo Tuđman agreed to the framework that became the Washington Agreement of 1 March 1994, establishing the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The order to the HVO to cease fire against the ARBiH came down from the Croatian capital.

That the war could be switched off by a directive from Zagreb confirmed what the ICTY Prlić et al. Trial Judgment (IT-04-74-T) found about the structure of the Herceg-Bosna project: its centre of gravity lay outside Bosnia. The HVO field commanders who had prosecuted the campaign in the Lašva Valley and around Mostar did not negotiate themselves out of the war; they were instructed out of it by the patron whose policy the campaign had served.

For the Herceg-Bosna leadership the directive was a moment of reckoning. Washington offered Croatia a path back toward international respectability and an eventual green light, the following year, for the Krajina operations that would reverse Serb gains. The price was the abandonment of the maximalist Herceg-Bosna project and the integration of Croat forces into a federation with the Bosniaks they had just been fighting. The local leadership’s preferences were, in the end, subordinate to the patron’s grand strategy.

The choice was therefore obedience or defiance at the moment the patron called the war off. To acknowledge Zagreb’s ceasefire order was to accept the Federation and the end of the independent Herceg-Bosna ambition — the path the historical record took. To resist it was to insist on a Bosnian Croat war that Croatia itself no longer wished to fund, a posture that could not be sustained once the sponsor had turned.
